subtopics.title: HTTP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to configure the Mule 4 HTTP Connector for building REST APIs with http:listener and calling external services with the http:request operation.
subtopics.summary: The HTTP Connector exposes REST endpoints with the listener operation and calls outbound web services with the request operation.
subtopics.content_html:
The HTTP Connector is the backbone of almost every MuleSoft integration: it exposes APIs for other systems to call and it calls out to external HTTP and HTTPS services. In Mule 4 it ships as a single connector with two primary operations, listener as a message source and request as a processor, both built on a shared configuration element.

HTTP Listener Configuration

An http:listener-config defines a reusable connection — host, port, and optional TLS context — that one or more http:listener sources reference. The listener source triggers a flow whenever a matching HTTP request arrives, and it exposes the incoming method, headers, query parameters, and URI parameters as part of the Mule event attributes.

<http:listener-config name="HTTP_Listener_config" basePath="/api">
    <http:listener-connection host="0.0.0.0" port="8081" />
</http:listener-config>

<flow name="get-orders-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/orders/{orderId}" allowedMethods="GET"/>
    <set-variable variableName="orderId" value="#[attributes.uriParams.orderId]"/>
    <db:select config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = :id</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{id: vars.orderId}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>
</flow>

HTTP Request Configuration

To call another HTTP service, define an http:request-config pointing at the target host, then use http:request processors to make individual calls, overriding the path, method, headers, or query parameters per call.

<http:request-config name="Payment_API_config">
    <http:request-connection host="payments.internal.example.com" port="443" protocol="HTTPS"/>
</http:request-config>

<flow name="charge-card-flow">
    <http:request config-ref="Payment_API_config" path="/v1/charges" method="POST">
        <http:headers>#[{'Content-Type': 'application/json'}]</http:headers>
        <http:body>#[payload]</http:body>
    </http:request>
    <choice>
        <when expression="#[attributes.statusCode == 200]">
            <logger message="Payment succeeded"/>
        </when>
        <otherwise>
            <raise-error type="PAYMENT:DECLINED" description="Charge failed"/>
        </otherwise>
    </choice>
</flow>

Key Attributes

AttributeApplies ToPurpose
basePathlistener-configPrefix shared by all listeners using this config
pathlistener / requestURI template, supports {uriParam} placeholders
allowedMethodslistenerRestricts which HTTP verbs trigger the flow
methodrequestHTTP verb used for the outbound call
responseTimeoutrequest-configMilliseconds to wait before failing the call
tlsContextlistener-config / request-configEnables HTTPS with key/trust stores

The response of an http:request populates payload with the response body and attributes.statusCode and attributes.headers with metadata, which is typically inspected in a <choice> router to branch on success or failure.

Note: APIkit Router, used for RAML/OAS-driven APIs, sits on top of an http:listener and dispatches incoming requests to flows named after the resource and method, so understanding the raw listener is foundational even when using APIkit.

Query Parameters and Headers

Incoming query parameters and headers are available on the listener side through attributes.queryParams and attributes.headers respectively, both exposed as case-insensitive multi-maps so a header can be read regardless of how the caller capitalized it. On the request side, http:query-params and http:headers elements let a script build the outbound request dynamically from variables or payload fields.

Connection Pooling and Reuse

Because establishing a new TCP connection for every outbound call is expensive, http:request-config maintains a connection pool internally and reuses connections to the same host across multiple requests. Reusing a single request-config for all calls to a given service, rather than creating one per flow, is a best practice that meaningfully improves throughput under load.

Key Points

  • listener-config and request-config are separate reusable global elements for inbound and outbound HTTP respectively.
  • Path templates support URI parameters accessed via attributes.uriParams.
  • Always check attributes.statusCode after an http:request since non-2xx responses do not always throw errors by default.
  • TLS contexts enable HTTPS for both inbound listeners and outbound requests.

subtopics.title: Database Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn to configure the Mule 4 Database Connector for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and stored procedure operations using parameterized SQL statements.
subtopics.summary: The Database Connector executes parameterized SQL against relational databases using dedicated operations for each statement type.
subtopics.content_html:
The Database Connector lets Mule applications read from and write to relational databases such as MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Derby. Rather than a single generic "execute SQL" operation, it provides distinct operations — select, insert, update, delete, bulk operations, and stored procedure calls — each with dedicated metadata support in Anypoint Studio.

Configuring the Connection

A db:config element holds connection details. Generic databases use a JDBC connection with a driver class name and URL, while several databases (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Derby) have dedicated connection types with simpler host/port/user fields and built-in connection pooling.

<db:config name="Database_Config" doc:name="Database Config">
    <db:my-sql-connection host="${db.host}" port="3306" user="${db.user}"
        password="${db.password}" database="orders_db">
        <db:pooling-profile maxPoolSize="10" minPoolSize="2"/>
    </db:my-sql-connection>
</db:config>

Parameterized SELECT and INSERT

Every operation accepts a SQL statement with named parameters prefixed by a colon, bound through the db:input-parameters element using a DataWeave map. This avoids string concatenation and protects against SQL injection.

<flow name="get-active-customers-flow">
    <db:select config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE status = :status AND created_at > :since</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{status: 'ACTIVE', since: vars.cutoffDate}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>
</flow>

<flow name="insert-order-flow">
    <db:insert config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total, created_at) VALUES (:customerId, :total, :createdAt)</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{
            customerId: payload.customerId,
            total: payload.total,
            createdAt: now()
        }]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:insert>
</flow>

Stored Procedures and Bulk Operations

The db:stored-procedure operation calls database procedures and can map OUT parameters back into the Mule event. db:bulk-insert and related bulk operations execute the same statement repeatedly for each item of an incoming array, which is far more efficient than looping over individual inserts for large datasets.

<db:stored-procedure config-ref="Database_Config">
    <db:sql>{ call recalc_customer_totals(:customerId, :newTotal) }</db:sql>
    <db:input-parameters>#[{customerId: vars.customerId}]</db:input-parameters>
</db:stored-procedure>

Key Attributes and Operations

OperationPurpose
db:selectRun a SELECT and return a stream or list of rows
db:insert / db:update / db:deleteRun DML statements and return affected row counts
db:bulk-insert / db:bulk-updateExecute a statement once per item in an array efficiently
db:stored-procedureInvoke a database stored procedure, including OUT parameters
db:transaction (transactional scope)Group multiple operations into a single commit/rollback unit
Tip: Wrap multiple related db operations in a Mule transactional scope when they must all succeed or all fail together, such as an order insert followed by inventory decrements.

Streaming Large Result Sets

By default, db:select returns a streaming result set rather than loading every row into memory at once, which matters when a query can return millions of rows. Pairing a streaming select with a <foreach> router or a Batch Job lets a flow process rows incrementally instead of exhausting heap memory on a single large in-memory collection.

Handling Connection Failures

A reconnection strategy on db:config controls how the connector responds when the database becomes temporarily unreachable, retrying the connection a configured number of times before the operation ultimately fails and propagates a DB:CONNECTIVITY error that a Mule error handler can catch.

Key Points

  • Always use named parameters (:name) with db:input-parameters instead of concatenating SQL strings.
  • Dedicated connection types (MySQL, Oracle, and so on) simplify configuration versus generic JDBC.
  • Bulk operations dramatically outperform per-row loops for large datasets.
  • Use transactions to guarantee atomicity across multiple related database operations.

subtopics.title: MySQL Database Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Database Connector for MySQL, including JDBC driver setup, db:my-sql-connection, connection pooling, and select/bulk-insert examples.
subtopics.summary: MySQL integration in Mule 4 uses the generic Database Connector with the MySQL JDBC driver and the db:my-sql-connection element.
subtopics.content_html:
Most enterprise integrations eventually need to read from or write to a relational database, and MySQL is one of the most common targets you'll wire into a Mule application. Rather than shipping a dedicated MySQL connector, MuleSoft handles this through the generic Database Connector, which speaks to MySQL over a standard JDBC driver. Typical use cases include synchronizing order records between a CRM and an e-commerce platform, staging data for a nightly batch load, looking up reference data mid-flow, or writing transformed payloads into a reporting schema.

Adding the MySQL Driver

Because the Database Connector is driver-agnostic, you must add the MySQL JDBC driver as a Maven dependency in your project's pom.xml before the connector can open a connection. Without it, deploying the application throws a ClassNotFoundException at runtime rather than a design-time error.

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <version>8.3.0</version>
</dependency>

Global Configuration

The connector exposes a dedicated db:my-sql-connection element that takes host, port, user, password, and database attributes directly, so you don't need to hand-craft a JDBC URL. Connection pooling is configured on the same element through the poolingProfile child, and credentials should always be externalized to a secure properties file rather than hardcoded.

<db:config name="MySQL_Config" doc:name="MySQL Config">
    <db:my-sql-connection host="${db.host}" port="${db.port}"
        user="${db.user}" password="${secure::db.password}"
        database="${db.database}">
        <db:pooling-profile maxPoolSize="10" minPoolSize="2" acquireIncrement="1"/>
    </db:my-sql-connection>
</db:config>

Key Operations

The Database Connector exposes a consistent set of operations regardless of the underlying vendor, which is one of its biggest strengths — you can swap MySQL for PostgreSQL or Oracle later with minimal flow changes.

OperationPurpose
db:selectRuns a parameterized SELECT and returns a streaming or in-memory result set
db:insertInserts a single row and can return generated keys
db:bulk-insertInserts a batch of rows from a collection payload in one round trip
db:update / db:deleteRuns parameterized UPDATE/DELETE statements
db:stored-procedureInvokes a stored procedure, including IN/OUT parameters

Example Flow

The flow below queries orders for a given status and then bulk-inserts an archive copy of any rows returned, all using bound parameters to avoid SQL injection.

<flow name="archive-shipped-orders">
    <db:select config-ref="MySQL_Config">
        <db:sql>SELECT id, customer_id, total, status FROM orders WHERE status = :status</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{status: 'SHIPPED'}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>

    <db:bulk-insert config-ref="MySQL_Config">
        <db:sql>INSERT INTO orders_archive (id, customer_id, total, status) VALUES (:id, :customer_id, :total, :status)</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[payload]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:bulk-insert>
</flow>
Tip: Always bind values with named parameters (:paramName) instead of concatenating DataWeave expressions into the SQL string. Concatenation defeats prepared-statement caching and opens the door to SQL injection.

Transactions

When a flow performs multiple write operations that must succeed or fail together, wrap them in a <try> scope with a transactional action, or set the transaction type at the operation level. The Database Connector participates in Mule's local transaction manager, so a rollback on error will undo every statement executed within the transactional boundary.

  • MySQL access goes through the generic Database Connector plus the MySQL JDBC driver, not a dedicated MySQL-only connector.
  • Use db:my-sql-connection for readable, vendor-specific connection attributes instead of a raw JDBC URL.
  • Always parameterize SQL with named bindings and store credentials in a secure properties file.
  • Use db:bulk-insert for batch writes and wrap multi-statement writes in a transaction when atomicity matters.

subtopics.title: File Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Mule 4 File Connector reads, writes, lists, and listens for files on the local file system, including matchers and streaming file reads.
subtopics.summary: The File Connector reads, writes, and watches files on a local or mounted file system, commonly used for batch integration patterns.
subtopics.content_html:
The File Connector integrates Mule applications with a local or network-mounted file system. It is frequently used to pick up inbound batch files, write processed output, or archive files after they have been consumed, and it pairs naturally with the Batch Job component for large file processing.

Configuring the Connector

An file:config element defines a working directory that all relative paths in operations resolve against, which keeps flows portable across environments.

<file:config name="File_Config">
    <file:connection workingDir="${file.workingDir}"/>
</file:config>

Reading and Listing Files

file:read reads a single known file into the payload as a stream, while file:list returns metadata and content for every file in a directory matching an optional matcher, which can filter by filename pattern, size, or modification date.

<flow name="list-incoming-files-flow">
    <file:list config-ref="File_Config" directoryPath="incoming">
        <file:matcher filenamePattern="*.csv"/>
    </file:list>
    <foreach>
        <logger message="Found file: #[payload.attributes.fileName]"/>
    </foreach>
</flow>

Listening for New or Updated Files

The file:on-new-or-updated-file source triggers a flow automatically whenever a file appears in or changes within a watched directory, making it the standard entry point for file-based integrations that should react in near real time.

<flow name="process-orders-file-flow">
    <file:listener config-ref="File_Config" directory="incoming" autoDelete="false">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="5000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <file:matcher filenamePattern="orders-*.csv"/>
    </file:listener>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
    <file:write config-ref="File_Config" path="processed/#[attributes.fileName]"/>
</flow>

Writing and Archiving

file:write creates or overwrites a file with the current payload, supporting a mode attribute (OVERWRITE, APPEND, or CREATE_NEW) to control collision behavior.

Key Attributes

AttributeOperationPurpose
workingDirconfigBase directory for relative paths
directory / directoryPathlistener / listFolder to watch or list
autoDeletelistenerDelete the file after successful processing
filenamePatternmatcherGlob-style pattern to filter file names
modewriteOVERWRITE, APPEND, or CREATE_NEW
Note: Because file:read and the file listener return streaming payloads by default, wrap consuming logic in a way that reads the stream only once, or configure repeatable streaming if the payload must be read multiple times.

File Locking and Concurrent Access

When multiple processes might touch the same directory, the File Connector can acquire a file lock during read operations to avoid processing a file that another process is still writing. This is particularly important in clustered CloudHub deployments where more than one worker could otherwise attempt to pick up the same inbound file simultaneously.

Combining with Batch Job

For large files containing many logical records — for instance, a CSV export with tens of thousands of rows — it is common to read the file once with file:read and then hand the parsed array off to a Batch Job, which splits the records into manageable steps, processes them with configurable parallelism, and aggregates the results at the end.

Key Points

  • All relative paths resolve against the workingDir configured on file:config.
  • file:on-new-or-updated-file is the standard trigger for reactive file processing pipelines.
  • Matchers filter which files are picked up by name pattern, size, or timestamp.
  • Use autoDelete or a move/archive step to prevent reprocessing the same file repeatedly.

subtopics.title: FTP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to configure the Mule 4 FTP Connector for polling remote directories, reading and writing files, and archiving processed files with ftp:listener.
subtopics.summary: The FTP Connector polls remote directories and reads or writes files using ftp:config, ftp:listener, ftp:read, and ftp:write.
subtopics.content_html:
File-based integration hasn't gone away, and plenty of trading partners, mainframes, and legacy systems still exchange data exclusively through FTP. The FTP Connector lets a Mule application poll a remote directory for new files, write output files, and manage file lifecycle operations like listing, renaming, and deleting — all without writing custom socket code.

Typical Use Cases

You'll reach for the FTP Connector when a partner drops nightly CSV extracts into a shared directory that Mule needs to pick up and transform, when a downstream mainframe batch job expects fixed-width files delivered on a schedule, or when an internal system publishes flat files that other applications consume asynchronously.

Global Configuration

The ftp:config element wraps an ftp:connection that carries the host, port, credentials, and working directory. Because plain FTP transmits credentials and data unencrypted, it should be reserved for internal networks or legacy systems that genuinely have no SFTP/FTPS option.

<ftp:config name="FTP_Config" doc:name="FTP Config">
    <ftp:connection host="${ftp.host}" port="${ftp.port}"
        username="${ftp.username}" password="${secure::ftp.password}"
        workingDir="/outbound" connectionTimeout="30" connectionTimeoutUnit="SECONDS"/>
</ftp:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
ftp:listenerMessage source that polls a directory and triggers a flow for each matching file
ftp:readReads a specific file into the payload as a stream
ftp:writeWrites the current payload to a remote file, with append or overwrite modes
ftp:listLists files in a directory, optionally filtered and recursive
ftp:copy / ftp:rename / ftp:deleteManages file lifecycle after processing

Example Flow

This flow polls an inbound directory every 60 seconds, converts each CSV to JSON, writes the result to an outbound directory, and then moves the source file into a processed folder so it isn't picked up twice.

<flow name="ftp-inbound-csv-flow">
    <ftp:listener config-ref="FTP_Config" directory="/inbound" autoDelete="false">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="60000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <ftp:matcher filenamePattern="*.csv"/>
    </ftp:listener>

    <ee:transform doc:name="CSV to JSON">
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>

    <ftp:write config-ref="FTP_Config" path="/outbound/#[attributes.fileName replace '.csv' with '.json']"/>

    <ftp:copy config-ref="FTP_Config" path="#[attributes.path]" targetPath="/processed" doc:name="Archive source file"/>
    <ftp:delete config-ref="FTP_Config" path="#[attributes.path]"/>
</flow>
Note: The ftp:listener attribute autoDelete removes the source file immediately after it's read into the flow. Set it to false when you need the original file available later in the flow for archiving, as shown above.

Error Handling and Reliability

Network blips are common with FTP, so configure reconnection strategies on the connection and consider a watermark or idempotent message filter if the same file could be reprocessed after a partial failure. For high-volume directories, prefer ftp:listener over manual polling with ftp:list, since the listener already tracks which files have been processed.

Choosing Between FTP and Its Secure Alternatives

Before settling on plain FTP, confirm the partner genuinely cannot support FTPS (FTP over TLS) or SFTP. Many "legacy" FTP requirements turn out to be a default configuration rather than a hard constraint, and moving to an encrypted transport removes an entire class of credential-exposure risk with only a small configuration change on the Mule side. Where FTP is unavoidable, isolate the traffic on a private network segment or VPN tunnel rather than exposing it over the open internet.

Note: The FTP Connector and the SFTP Connector share a very similar operation set — read, write, list, listener — which makes migrating a flow from FTP to SFTP largely a matter of swapping the config element and connection attributes rather than rewriting flow logic.
  • FTP is unencrypted; use it only for trusted internal networks or when a partner has no SFTP/FTPS alternative.
  • The ftp:listener source handles polling and file-matching so you don't have to build your own scheduler around ftp:list.
  • Always plan a post-processing strategy — move, rename, or delete — so files aren't reprocessed on the next poll.
  • Evaluate FTPS or SFTP first; the operation set is similar enough that migrating later is straightforward.

subtopics.title: SFTP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 SFTP Connector with password or SSH key-based authentication, sftp:listener watermarking, and full read/write flow examples in XML.
subtopics.summary: The SFTP Connector securely transfers files over SSH using sftp:config with password or identity-file authentication and the listener, read, and write operations.
subtopics.content_html:
SFTP is the connector you'll actually use in production far more often than plain FTP, since it layers file transfer on top of the SSH protocol and encrypts both the authentication handshake and the data in transit. Anywhere a business partner requires a secure file drop — EDI documents, payment batches, healthcare claims — SFTP is the de facto standard, and Mule's SFTP Connector supports both password and public-key authentication out of the box.

Global Configuration

An sftp:config wraps an sftp:connection. Port 22 is the SSH default, and you can authenticate either with a username/password pair or, more securely, with a private key file referenced through identityFile and an optional passphrase.

<sftp:config name="SFTP_Config" doc:name="SFTP Config">
    <sftp:connection host="${sftp.host}" port="22"
        username="${sftp.username}"
        identityFile="${sftp.keyPath}"
        passphrase="${secure::sftp.keyPassphrase}"
        connectionTimeout="30" connectionTimeoutUnit="SECONDS">
        <reconnection>
            <reconnect frequency="5000" count="3"/>
        </reconnection>
    </sftp:connection>
</sftp:config>

For simple password authentication, swap identityFile/passphrase for a password attribute pointing at a secure property. Most partner integrations, however, will supply you with a private key and ask for your public key to be added to their authorized_keys file.

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
sftp:listenerMessage source that watches a directory and fires per new/modified file
sftp:readStreams a remote file's contents into the payload
sftp:writeWrites the payload to a remote path, supporting OVERWRITE, APPEND, and fail if exists modes
sftp:listLists directory contents with optional recursion and matcher filters
sftp:delete / sftp:renameCleans up or archives files after processing

Example Flow

The flow below listens for new invoice files, validates the payload against a schema, and writes the confirmed file to an outbound directory for a downstream ERP pickup.

<flow name="sftp-invoice-inbound-flow">
    <sftp:listener config-ref="SFTP_Config" directory="/partner/inbound" watermarkEnabled="true">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="30000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <sftp:matcher filenamePattern="invoice-*.xml"/>
    </sftp:listener>

    <validation:is-true expression="#[payload startsWith '<Invoice'"]" doc:name="Basic shape check"/>

    <sftp:write config-ref="SFTP_Config"
        path="/erp/outbound/#[attributes.fileName]"
        mode="OVERWRITE"/>
</flow>
Tip: Enable watermarkEnabled="true" on sftp:listener so Mule only processes files newer than the last recorded timestamp. This prevents reprocessing the entire directory after an application restart.

Security Considerations

Prefer key-based authentication over passwords whenever the partner supports it, and rotate keys according to your organization's security policy. Store the private key and any passphrase outside of source control — typically in a secrets manager or an encrypted properties file — and restrict the SFTP user's home directory with chroot on the server side if you control it.

Working with High-Volume or Large-File Transfers

The sftp:read and sftp:write operations stream by default, so large files — multi-gigabyte exports, for instance — don't need to fit entirely in heap memory. When a directory listener has to process thousands of files per cycle, tune maxConcurrency on the containing flow to control how many transfers run in parallel, since opening too many simultaneous SSH sessions against the same remote server can trigger rate limiting or connection refusals on the partner's side.

Tip: If a remote server enforces strict host key checking, configure a known-hosts file on the connection rather than disabling host key verification; skipping verification defeats much of the security benefit SFTP provides in the first place.
  • SFTP encrypts both credentials and payload over SSH, making it the preferred choice over plain FTP for partner integrations.
  • Use identityFile and passphrase for key-based authentication instead of passwords when possible.
  • Turn on watermarking in sftp:listener to avoid reprocessing files after a redeploy or restart.
  • Stream large files by default and tune maxConcurrency to avoid overwhelming the remote server.

subtopics.title: Amazon S3 Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Amazon S3 Connector with access-key or IAM role authentication, then use the create-object, get-object, and list-objects operations.
subtopics.summary: The Amazon S3 Connector reads, writes, lists, and deletes objects in S3 buckets using s3:config with static credentials or an IAM instance role.
subtopics.content_html:
Cloud object storage has become a default landing zone for everything from data lake ingestion to document archival, and Amazon S3 is the most widely used implementation. The Amazon S3 Connector lets a Mule flow create, retrieve, list, copy, and delete objects in a bucket, making it a natural fit for staging files before a batch job, archiving processed documents, or serving as the backing store for a document management API.

Typical Use Cases

Common patterns include landing inbound files from a partner into a raw bucket before transformation, writing generated PDFs or reports for later retrieval, archiving processed SFTP files for compliance retention, and building a lightweight file API on top of S3 pre-signed URLs.

Global Configuration

The s3:config element wraps a connection that authenticates either with a static access key/secret key pair or, in EC2/ECS deployments, with an IAM instance role and no static credentials at all. When static credentials are used, they should always be pulled from a secure properties file rather than embedded in the flow.

<s3:config name="S3_Config" doc:name="S3 Config">
    <s3:connection accessKey="${s3.accessKey}" secretKey="${secure::s3.secretKey}"
        region="US_EAST_1"/>
</s3:config>
Tip: When running on AWS compute with an attached IAM role, omit accessKey/secretKey entirely and let the connector fall back to the default AWS credentials provider chain. This avoids storing long-lived secrets altogether.

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
s3:create-objectUploads a payload as a new object under a given key
s3:get-objectRetrieves an object's content as a stream
s3:list-objectsLists object keys in a bucket, optionally filtered by prefix
s3:copy-objectCopies an object within or across buckets
s3:delete-objectRemoves an object by key
s3:create-presigned-uriGenerates a temporary, signed download/upload URL

Example Flow

This flow lists objects under a prefix representing today's inbound batch, then downloads and republishes each one for downstream processing.

<flow name="s3-process-daily-batch">
    <s3:list-objects config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-inbound"
        prefix="batch/#[now() as String {format: 'yyyy-MM-dd'}]/"/>

    <foreach>
        <s3:get-object config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-inbound"
            key="#[payload.key]" target="fileContent"/>

        <s3:create-object config-ref="S3_Config" bucketName="acme-processed"
            key="processed/#[payload.key]"
            body="#[vars.fileContent]"/>
    </foreach>
</flow>

Performance and Cost Notes

For large objects, favor streaming (the default for s3:get-object) over loading the full payload into memory, and set an explicit storageClass on s3:create-object when writing archival data to control cost. Batch listing operations with pagination (maxKeys) when a bucket may contain more objects than fit comfortably in one response.

Securing Access to a Bucket

Scope the IAM policy attached to your access key or instance role as tightly as possible — grant only the actions the flow actually needs, such as s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on a specific bucket prefix, rather than broad account-wide S3 permissions. When external parties need temporary access to a single object, generate a time-limited link with s3:create-presigned-uri instead of sharing bucket credentials, and keep the expiration window as short as the use case allows.

Tip: Enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) on buckets holding sensitive data, and configure the connector's create-object operation to set the appropriate encryption headers rather than relying solely on bucket-level defaults.
  • Prefer IAM instance roles over static access keys when the Mule app runs on AWS infrastructure.
  • Use s3:list-objects with a prefix filter to scope operations instead of scanning an entire bucket.
  • Stream large objects rather than buffering them fully in memory during get-object/create-object.
  • Scope IAM permissions narrowly and prefer presigned URLs over shared credentials for temporary external access.

subtopics.title: Azure Service Bus Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Azure Service Bus Connector for queues and topics, including publish, listener, and peek-lock complete and abandon message examples.
subtopics.summary: The Azure Service Bus Connector publishes and consumes messages from Azure queues and topics using a connection string and peek-lock message handling.
subtopics.content_html:
Organizations standardized on Microsoft Azure frequently use Azure Service Bus as their enterprise messaging backbone, and the Azure Service Bus Connector lets Mule applications publish and consume messages from that same infrastructure without introducing a second broker. It supports both the simple queue point-to-point pattern and the publish/subscribe pattern through topics and subscriptions, which makes it suitable for anything from order processing pipelines to fan-out event notification.

Queues vs. Topics and Subscriptions

A queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer, which suits classic request-processing workloads such as a single order-fulfillment service reading orders one at a time. A topic, by contrast, broadcasts each message to every subscription registered on it, so multiple independent consumers — say, billing, shipping, and analytics — can each process the same event without competing for it.

Global Configuration

The connector authenticates using either a full connection string (containing a Shared Access Signature key) copied from the Azure portal, or individual SAS policy name/key pairs. The connection string approach is the most common because Azure generates it for you directly against the namespace or entity.

<azure-service-bus:config name="ServiceBus_Config" doc:name="Azure Service Bus Config">
    <azure-service-bus:connection connectionString="${secure::asb.connectionString}"/>
</azure-service-bus:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
azure-service-bus:publishSends a message to a queue or topic
azure-service-bus:on-new-message-listenerMessage source that consumes from a queue or a topic subscription
azure-service-bus:complete-messageAcknowledges a message so it is removed from the entity (peek-lock mode)
azure-service-bus:abandon-messageReleases the lock and returns the message to the entity for redelivery
azure-service-bus:dead-letter-messageMoves a poison message to the dead-letter sub-queue

Example Flow

This flow publishes an order-created event to a topic, and a second flow consumes it from a dedicated subscription, completing the message only after successful processing.

<flow name="publish-order-event">
    <azure-service-bus:publish config-ref="ServiceBus_Config"
        destination="orders-topic" destinationType="TOPIC">
        <azure-service-bus:body>#[write(payload, 'application/json')]</azure-service-bus:body>
    </azure-service-bus:publish>
</flow>

<flow name="consume-billing-subscription">
    <azure-service-bus:on-new-message-listener config-ref="ServiceBus_Config"
        destination="orders-topic" subscriptionName="billing-subscription"
        receiveAndDeleteModeEnabled="false"/>

    <try>
        <flow-ref name="process-billing-event"/>
        <azure-service-bus:complete-message lockToken="#[attributes.lockToken]"/>
    <error-handler>
        <on-error-continue>
            <azure-service-bus:abandon-message lockToken="#[attributes.lockToken]"/>
        </on-error-continue>
    </error-handler>
    </try>
</flow>
Note: Leaving receiveAndDeleteModeEnabled false puts the entity in peek-lock mode, meaning a message stays invisible but not removed until you explicitly complete, abandon, or dead-letter it. This gives you at-least-once delivery semantics with room to retry.

Sizing and Tier Considerations

Azure Service Bus is offered in Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers, and the tier you provision directly affects which features are available to your Mule flows. Topics and sessions, for instance, require at least the Standard tier, so confirm the namespace tier matches the entity types your integration design assumes before you build against it. Premium namespaces add dedicated throughput and larger message sizes, which matters for high-volume event pipelines moving large payloads.

When a consuming flow needs strict message ordering within a logical group — for example, all events for a single order — enable sessions on the queue or subscription and set a sessionId on publish so Service Bus routes related messages to the same consumer in order.

  • Choose queues for point-to-point workloads and topics/subscriptions when multiple independent consumers need the same event.
  • Peek-lock mode plus explicit completion is the safest default for reliable processing; avoid receive-and-delete unless duplicate loss is acceptable.
  • Store the Service Bus connection string as a secure property, never inline in the flow XML.
  • Confirm your namespace tier supports the entity types (topics, sessions) your flow design depends on.

subtopics.title: Salesforce Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Mule 4 Salesforce Connector authenticates, runs SOQL queries, performs create, update, and upsert DML, and subscribes to platform events.
subtopics.summary: The Salesforce Connector authenticates via OAuth and exposes SOQL queries, DML operations, and streaming event subscriptions.
subtopics.content_html:
Salesforce is one of the most common systems integrated with MuleSoft, and the Salesforce Connector wraps the Salesforce SOAP, REST, Bulk, and Streaming APIs behind a consistent set of Mule operations. It handles authentication, session management, and API versioning so flows can focus on business logic rather than raw HTTP calls to Salesforce endpoints.

Authenticating

The connector supports several authentication types, most commonly username/password combined with a security token appended to the password, and OAuth 2.0 JWT bearer flow for production integrations that avoid storing a static password. The chosen method is set on the salesforce:config global element.

<salesforce:config name="Salesforce_Config">
    <salesforce:basic-connection username="${sfdc.username}"
        password="${sfdc.password}${sfdc.securityToken}"
        securityToken=""
        consumerKey="${sfdc.consumerKey}"
        consumerSecret="${sfdc.consumerSecret}"/>
</salesforce:config>

Querying with SOQL

salesforce:query executes a SOQL statement and returns matching records as a stream of objects, which can be further transformed with DataWeave.

<flow name="get-open-opportunities-flow">
    <salesforce:query config-ref="Salesforce_Config">
        <salesforce:salesforce-query><![CDATA[SELECT Id, Name, Amount, StageName FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName != 'Closed Won' AND StageName != 'Closed Lost']]></salesforce:salesforce-query>
    </salesforce:query>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (opp) -> {
  id: opp.Id,
  name: opp.Name,
  amount: opp.Amount
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Create, Update and Upsert

DML operations accept an array of objects and a type name, and upsert additionally requires an external ID field to match existing records, which is ideal for idempotent synchronization from an external system of record.

<salesforce:upsert config-ref="Salesforce_Config" type="Contact" externalIdFieldName="External_Id__c">
    <salesforce:records>#[[{
        External_Id__c: payload.customerId,
        FirstName: payload.firstName,
        LastName: payload.lastName,
        Email: payload.email
    }]]</salesforce:records>
</salesforce:upsert>

Subscribing to Events

For real-time integrations, salesforce:subscribe-topic or Change Data Capture subscriptions listen for Platform Events or record changes over Salesforce's Streaming API, triggering a flow the moment a change occurs in Salesforce rather than relying on scheduled polling.

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
salesforce:query / query-singleRun SOQL to retrieve records
salesforce:create / update / upsert / deleteStandard DML against one or more sObjects
salesforce:bulk-insert / bulk-updateHigh-volume operations via the Bulk API
salesforce:subscribe-topicListen for Streaming API / Platform Events
Note: Salesforce enforces API call limits per org per 24-hour period, so bulk operations and CDC/Streaming subscriptions are usually preferred over frequent SOQL polling for high-volume integrations.

Handling Salesforce-Specific Errors

DML operations can partially succeed, returning a result array where some records saved and others failed validation rules or triggers on the Salesforce side. A well-built integration inspects each result entry individually rather than assuming the entire batch either fully succeeded or fully failed, logging or retrying only the records that actually errored.

Metadata-Driven Development

Anypoint Studio can connect to a Salesforce org and pull field-level metadata directly into the DataWeave editor, offering autocomplete for standard and custom fields on any sObject. This significantly reduces mapping errors compared to typing field API names from memory, especially in orgs with many custom fields ending in __c.

Key Points

  • salesforce:config centralizes authentication so individual operations stay focused on business logic.
  • upsert with an external ID field is the standard pattern for idempotent record synchronization.
  • Bulk operations reduce API consumption compared to looping over single-record DML calls.
  • Streaming subscriptions enable near real-time reaction to Salesforce data changes.

subtopics.title: Workday Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Workday Connector for RaaS reports and SOAP-based HR and Financials integrations, with authentication and flow examples.
subtopics.summary: The Workday Connector integrates Mule applications with Workday HCM and Financials through Reports-as-a-Service and the underlying SOAP web services.
subtopics.content_html:
Workday is a cloud platform for Human Capital Management (HCM) and Financial Management that many enterprises treat as the system of record for employee, payroll, and financial data. Because Workday exposes almost everything through XML/SOAP-based web services rather than a conventional REST API, integrating with it by hand is tedious — the Workday Connector wraps that complexity into a small set of Mule 4 operations so integration developers do not have to hand-build SOAP envelopes for every call.

Two Integration Styles

Workday exposes two integration surfaces that the connector supports differently:

  • Reports-as-a-Service (RaaS) — custom or standard Workday reports published with a web service endpoint and consumed as XML or JSON over HTTP. This is the fastest path for pulling worker, position, or organization data without dealing with raw SOAP schemas.
  • Workday Web Services (SOAP) — the full set of Workday operations (Human Resources, Financial Management, Payroll, Integrations) delivered as WSDL-described SOAP services, useful when RaaS does not cover a required create or update operation.

Most projects use workday-raas:config for read-heavy reporting integrations and fall back to the SOAP web services (often through the Web Service Consumer connector or a dedicated Workday SOAP module) for transactional writes such as hiring, terminations, or compensation changes.

Global Configuration

A Workday RaaS configuration needs the tenant name, the Workday host, and a service account with the appropriate security group access assigned in Workday itself — connector configuration alone cannot grant field-level permissions.

AttributePurpose
username / passwordIntegration System User (ISU) credentials configured in Workday, typically with a dedicated integration security group
tenantNameThe Workday tenant identifier, e.g. acme_gms
hostThe Workday API host, e.g. wd5-impl-services1.workday.com for a sandbox environment
connectionTimeout / responseTimeoutGuards against slow report generation on large data sets
Tip: Request a dedicated Integration System User and security group from your Workday functional team rather than reusing a human user's credentials — ISUs are exempt from password expiry policies that would otherwise break scheduled integrations.

Key Operations

  • Execute Report — invokes a published RaaS report by name, passing report parameters (effective date, organization, worker status) as key-value pairs and returning the result as XML or JSON depending on how the report was published.
  • Get Workers / custom report operations — generated dynamically based on the reports exposed to the configured tenant, since RaaS reports are effectively custom operations per tenant.

Example Flow

The following flow calls a custom Workday report that returns active workers for a given supervisory organization, then maps the response into a canonical worker record with DataWeave.

<workday-raas:config name="Workday_RaaS_Config">
    <workday-raas:connection
        username="${workday.isu.username}"
        password="${workday.isu.password}"
        tenantName="${workday.tenant}"
        host="${workday.host}"/>
</workday-raas:config>

<flow name="get-active-workers-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/workers/{orgId}"/>
    <workday-raas:execute-report
        config-ref="Workday_RaaS_Config"
        reportName="RaaS_Active_Workers_By_Org">
        <workday-raas:report-parameters>
            #[{ 'Supervisory_Organization': attributes.uriParams.orgId }]
        </workday-raas:report-parameters>
    </workday-raas:execute-report>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.Report_Entry map (worker) -> {
    employeeId: worker.Worker_ID,
    firstName: worker.First_Name,
    lastName: worker.Last_Name,
    orgId: worker.Supervisory_Organization_Reference.ID
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Common Use Cases

  • Syncing new hires and terminations from Workday HCM into downstream identity and provisioning systems.
  • Feeding payroll or GL data from Workday Financials into a data warehouse or ERP.
  • Building an employee self-service API layer over Workday reports for internal portals.

Key Points

  • RaaS is the lightest-weight option for read access; SOAP web services are required for most write operations.
  • Report availability and parameters are tenant-specific and must be published and shared with the ISU security group before the connector can see them.
  • Always externalize tenant, host, and credentials to a secure properties file per environment (sandbox, preview, production).

subtopics.title: SAP Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Mule 4 SAP Connector uses JCo to call BAPIs and RFC function modules, plus IDoc handling and connection configuration.
subtopics.summary: The SAP Connector uses the SAP Java Connector (JCo) to invoke BAPIs, RFC function modules, and process IDocs from Mule applications.
subtopics.content_html:
SAP ECC and S/4HANA remain the backbone ERP for order management, finance, and materials planning at a large share of enterprises, and MuleSoft's SAP Connector is the standard bridge into that world. Rather than talking to SAP over plain HTTP, the connector communicates through the SAP Java Connector (JCo), a native library that speaks SAP's proprietary RFC (Remote Function Call) protocol directly to an SAP Application Server or SAP Gateway.

Prerequisites: JCo Libraries

Because JCo includes platform-specific native binaries licensed by SAP, it is not bundled with the connector or published to Anypoint Exchange. Before the SAP Connector will run, you must download the sapjco3.jar and matching native library for your OS from the SAP Support Portal (an SAP account is required) and install them into your local Maven repository, then reference them as a project dependency. This step catches most teams off guard the first time they add the connector.

Note: JCo versions are tied to specific SAP kernel and NetWeaver releases. Confirm the required JCo version with your SAP Basis team before installing, since a mismatch causes cryptic connection failures at runtime rather than at design time.

Global Configuration

The connector's global configuration mirrors the parameters an SAP GUI logon screen asks for, because it is establishing the same kind of RFC connection an SAP client would.

AttributePurpose
jco.client.ashostApplication server hostname
jco.client.sysnrSAP system number, e.g. 00
jco.client.clientSAP client (mandant), e.g. 800
jco.client.user / jco.client.passwdService account credentials with authorization to the target BAPIs
jco.client.langLogon language, e.g. EN
jco.destination.pool_capacity / peak_limitConnection pool sizing for concurrent RFC calls

Key Operations

  • Execute — invokes a named BAPI or RFC-enabled function module (for example BAPI_SALESORDER_CREATEFROMDAT2 or BAPI_MATERIAL_GET_DETAIL), passing import parameters and structures and returning export parameters, tables, and any BAPI return messages.
  • Listener for IDocs — the connector can also register as an IDoc listener, receiving inbound IDocs (Intermediate Documents) pushed from SAP for asynchronous, high-volume document exchange such as purchase orders or invoices.
  • Transaction (BAPI commit) — many BAPIs stage changes that require an explicit BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT call afterward, which the connector exposes as its own operation since SAP's transactional model does not auto-commit.

Example Flow

<sap:config name="SAP_Config">
    <sap:jco-connection
        ashost="${sap.ashost}"
        sysnr="${sap.sysnr}"
        client="${sap.client}"
        user="${sap.user}"
        passwd="${sap.password}"
        lang="EN"/>
</sap:config>

<flow name="get-material-details-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/materials/{materialId}"/>
    <sap:execute config-ref="SAP_Config" function="BAPI_MATERIAL_GET_DETAIL">
        <sap:imports>
            #[{ 'MATERIAL': attributes.uriParams.materialId }]
        </sap:imports>
    </sap:execute>
    <choice>
        <when expression="#[payload.RETURN.TYPE == 'E']">
            <raise-error type="SAP:MATERIAL_NOT_FOUND" description="#[payload.RETURN.MESSAGE]"/>
        </when>
        <otherwise>
            <ee:transform>
                <ee:message>
                    <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
    materialNumber: payload.MATERIALDATA.MATERIAL,
    description: payload.MATERIALDATA.MATL_DESC,
    baseUnit: payload.MATERIALDATA.BASE_UOM
}]]></ee:set-payload>
                </ee:message>
            </ee:transform>
        </otherwise>
    </choice>
</flow>

Common Use Cases

  • Exposing SAP master data (materials, customers, vendors) as REST APIs for e-commerce or portal applications.
  • Creating sales orders or purchase requisitions in SAP from external ordering systems.
  • Bridging IDoc-based EDI flows between SAP and trading partners or middleware.

Key Points

  • JCo native libraries must be sourced from SAP and added to the project separately — they cannot be redistributed with the connector.
  • BAPI return structures use a RETURN table with TYPE codes (E, W, S) rather than HTTP status codes; always check RETURN before treating a call as successful.
  • Remember explicit commits for BAPIs that stage changes rather than applying them immediately.

subtopics.title: ServiceNow Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 ServiceNow Connector to query, create, and update incidents and CMDB records through the Table API with OAuth2 or basic auth.
subtopics.summary: The ServiceNow Connector wraps the ServiceNow REST Table API so Mule flows can query and manage incidents, CMDB records, and other tables directly.
subtopics.content_html:
ServiceNow is the system of record for IT service management at many organizations, covering incidents, change requests, problems, and the configuration management database (CMDB). Integration teams typically need to either push events into ServiceNow — opening an incident when a monitoring system detects a failure — or pull ServiceNow data into other systems for reporting and automation. The ServiceNow Connector for Mule 4 (built on the REST-based Table API) covers both directions without requiring hand-rolled HTTP requests and pagination logic.

Global Configuration

Unlike the older SOAP-based ServiceNow integration style, the current connector generation talks to the REST Table API and the Import Set API, authenticating with either basic authentication or OAuth 2.0, depending on what the target instance's security policy allows.

AttributePurpose
instanceUrl (or instanceId)The instance base URL, e.g. https://acme.service-now.com
username / passwordBasic auth credentials for a dedicated integration user
clientId / clientSecretUsed with the OAuth2 grant type when the instance requires token-based auth
tokenUrlOAuth token endpoint, typically /oauth_token.do on the instance
Tip: Create a dedicated integration user with an explicit role assignment (for example, a custom role scoped only to the tables the integration touches) rather than granting the broad `admin` role — this keeps the blast radius small if credentials leak.

Key Operations

  • Query Records — retrieves records from any table using ServiceNow's encoded query syntax, with support for field selection and pagination via sysparm_limit and sysparm_offset.
  • Create Record — inserts a new record (an incident, a CI, a change request) into a specified table, returning the generated sys_id.
  • Update Record — performs a PATCH-style update against an existing record identified by sys_id.
  • Delete Record — removes a record, typically restricted to administrative integration flows.

Example Flow

This flow receives an alert payload from a monitoring system and opens a ServiceNow incident, then reads back the assignment group for confirmation.

<servicenow-rest:config name="ServiceNow_Config">
    <servicenow-rest:basic-connection
        instanceUrl="${servicenow.instanceUrl}"
        username="${servicenow.username}"
        password="${servicenow.password}"/>
</servicenow-rest:config>

<flow name="create-incident-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/incidents"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
    short_description: payload.alertSummary,
    urgency: if (payload.severity == 'critical') '1' else '3',
    category: 'software',
    caller_id: payload.reportedBy
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
    <servicenow-rest:create-record
        config-ref="ServiceNow_Config"
        tableName="incident"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ incidentNumber: payload.result.number, sysId: payload.result.sys_id }]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Querying with Encoded Queries

ServiceNow's encoded query syntax lets a single query string combine multiple field filters, comparisons, and sort orders without building a complex request body. A query such as active=true^priority=1^assignment_group=network_ops retrieves only high-priority open incidents assigned to a specific group, and the connector passes this straight through as the sysparm_query parameter. Pushing filtering logic to ServiceNow this way is significantly more efficient than retrieving broad result sets and filtering them afterward in DataWeave, especially against tables with millions of rows such as the CMDB's cmdb_ci table.

Common Use Cases

  • Auto-creating incidents from APM or monitoring tool alerts (Splunk, Datadog, PagerDuty) via API.
  • Synchronizing CMDB configuration items with an external asset inventory or discovery tool.
  • Exposing change request status through a self-service API for internal developer portals.
  • Closing the loop on automated remediation by updating incident state and work notes once a fix completes.

Key Points

  • The Table API works against any table by name, so the same operations handle incidents, problems, changes, and custom tables interchangeably.
  • Use encoded queries (sysparm_query) for efficient server-side filtering instead of pulling large result sets and filtering in DataWeave.
  • Prefer OAuth2 over basic auth where the instance supports it, especially for production integrations subject to security review.
  • Watch ServiceNow's REST API rate limits on shared/sub-production instances, and add retry logic with backoff for 429 responses during bulk synchronization jobs.

subtopics.title: NetSuite Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 NetSuite Connector with token-based authentication for SuiteTalk operations like get, add, and search on customer and order records.
subtopics.summary: The NetSuite Connector integrates Mule applications with NetSuite ERP through SuiteTalk web services using token-based authentication and record operations.
subtopics.content_html:
NetSuite is a cloud ERP and accounting platform widely used by mid-market and fast-growing companies for order management, inventory, and financials, and it exposes its data model through SuiteTalk, a set of SOAP (and, more recently, REST) web services built around a large catalog of record types — customer, salesOrder, item, invoice, and dozens more. The NetSuite Connector packages SuiteTalk access into Mule-friendly operations so integration developers work with familiar record and search DataWeave structures instead of raw SOAP payloads.

Global Configuration and Authentication

Modern NetSuite integrations should use Token-Based Authentication (TBA) rather than the legacy email/password/role combination, since TBA avoids storing a user's interactive credentials and survives password rotation and two-factor policies without breaking scheduled integrations.

AttributePurpose
accountThe NetSuite account ID, e.g. 1234567_SB1 for a sandbox account
consumerKey / consumerSecretIdentify the integration record created in NetSuite under Setup > Integration
tokenId / tokenSecretIssued to a specific NetSuite user/role pair, scoping what the integration can access
applicationIdLegacy web services application ID, still required by some endpoints/versions
endpoint / apiVersionThe SuiteTalk WSDL endpoint and schema version, e.g. 2023_2
Note: The role assigned to the token determines which record types and permissions (view, create, edit, full) the integration has — configure a dedicated integration role in NetSuite rather than reusing an administrator role.

Key Operations

  • Get — retrieves a single record by internal ID and record type.
  • Add — creates a new record, such as a salesOrder or customer, returning the generated internal ID.
  • Update / Upsert — modifies an existing record or creates it if it does not already exist, matched by internal ID or external ID.
  • Search — runs a structured search against a record type using field-level search criteria (equality, date ranges, text contains), returning paged result sets for large data volumes.

Example Flow

<netsuite:config name="NetSuite_Config">
    <netsuite:token-connection
        account="${netsuite.account}"
        consumerKey="${netsuite.consumerKey}"
        consumerSecret="${netsuite.consumerSecret}"
        tokenId="${netsuite.tokenId}"
        tokenSecret="${netsuite.tokenSecret}"
        applicationId="${netsuite.applicationId}"/>
</netsuite:config>

<flow name="create-sales-order-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/sales-orders"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/java
---
{
    entity: { internalId: payload.customerId },
    itemList: {
        item: payload.lineItems map (li) -> {
            item: { internalId: li.itemId },
            quantity: li.quantity
        }
    }
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
    <netsuite:add config-ref="NetSuite_Config" recordType="salesOrder"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ orderInternalId: payload.internalId, status: payload.status }]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Handling Governance and Concurrency Limits

NetSuite enforces per-account concurrency and governance limits on SuiteTalk requests, and bursty integration traffic can hit these limits during batch jobs such as nightly order synchronization. Design flows to process records in reasonably sized batches with the Batch component, and use the Until Successful scope around individual NetSuite calls to retry transient governance errors with exponential backoff rather than failing the entire batch on a single throttled request. For very high-volume extracts, prefer the search operation's paged results over repeated get calls per record, since search amortizes the per-request overhead across many records at once.

Common Use Cases

  • Pushing e-commerce or CRM orders into NetSuite as sales orders in near real time.
  • Synchronizing customer and item master data between NetSuite and a CRM or PIM system.
  • Extracting financial transactions from NetSuite into a data warehouse for reporting.
  • Reconciling inventory levels between NetSuite and a separate warehouse management system.

Key Points

  • Token-Based Authentication is the recommended approach; avoid storing interactive user passwords for integration accounts.
  • Search operations page through large result sets by design — always handle the searchId/pageIndex pattern for result sets beyond the default page size.
  • Match the apiVersion configured in the connector to the SuiteTalk schema version your NetSuite account supports to avoid field mapping errors after account upgrades.
  • Batch and throttle high-volume jobs to stay within NetSuite's concurrency governance limits rather than firing requests as fast as the flow allows.

subtopics.title: Email Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Email Connector's SMTP, IMAP, and POP3 elements to send mail, poll inboxes for new messages, and process email attachments correctly.
subtopics.summary: The Email Connector sends mail through email:smtp-config and receives it through email:imap-config or email:pop3-config, including attachment handling.
subtopics.content_html:
Email remains a surprisingly common integration surface — sending transactional notifications, routing inbound support requests into a case management system, or processing invoices that partners still send as attachments. The Email Connector covers both directions: an SMTP configuration for sending mail and IMAP or POP3 configurations for retrieving it, each modeled as separate global elements since sending and receiving use fundamentally different protocols.

Sending Email with SMTP

The email:smtp-config element defines the outbound mail server connection, including host, port, credentials, and whether to use STARTTLS. Most modern providers require authentication and encryption, so a typical configuration enables TLS on port 587.

<email:smtp-config name="SMTP_Config" doc:name="SMTP Config">
    <email:smtp-connection host="${smtp.host}" port="587"
        user="${smtp.user}" password="${secure::smtp.password}">
        <email:client-tls-context>
            <tls:trust-store insecure="false"/>
        </email:client-tls-context>
    </email:smtp-connection>
</email:smtp-config>

Receiving Email with IMAP or POP3

Use email:imap-config when you need to browse folders, search, and leave messages on the server after reading — the more capable and commonly used protocol. Use email:pop3-config for simpler mailboxes where messages are downloaded and typically removed from the server.

<email:imap-config name="IMAP_Config" doc:name="IMAP Config">
    <email:imap-connection host="${imap.host}" port="993"
        user="${imap.user}" password="${secure::imap.password}">
        <email:client-tls-context>
            <tls:trust-store insecure="false"/>
        </email:client-tls-context>
    </email:imap-connection>
</email:imap-config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
email:sendSends an email, optionally with attachments and HTML body
email:list-imap / email:list-pop3Retrieves messages from a mailbox, with filtering by criteria such as unread or subject
email:on-new-email-listenerMessage source that triggers a flow when new mail arrives
email:mark-as-read / email:deleteManages message state after processing to avoid reprocessing

Example Flow

This flow polls an inbox for unread messages with attachments, extracts each attachment for downstream processing, and sends a confirmation email once complete.

<flow name="process-invoice-inbox">
    <email:on-new-email-listener config-ref="IMAP_Config" mailboxFolder="INBOX">
        <scheduling-strategy>
            <fixed-frequency frequency="60000"/>
        </scheduling-strategy>
        <email:matcher subjectRegex="Invoice.*" hasAttachments="true"/>
    </email:on-new-email-listener>

    <foreach collection="#[payload.attachments]">
        <flow-ref name="store-invoice-attachment"/>
    </foreach>

    <email:send config-ref="SMTP_Config" subject="Invoice received" toAddresses="#[[attributes.from[0].address]]">
        <email:body contentType="text/plain"><![CDATA[Thanks, your invoice has been received and is being processed.]]></email:body>
    </email:send>

    <email:mark-as-read config-ref="IMAP_Config" emailId="#[attributes.id]"/>
</flow>
Note: Attachments arrive as a collection of parts on the payload, each with its own content type and stream; iterate over payload.attachments rather than assuming a single attachment per message.

Practical Considerations

Always mark messages as read or move them to a processed folder after handling them, otherwise a polling listener will pick up the same email on every cycle. For outbound mail at scale, consider a dedicated transactional email provider's API instead of raw SMTP, since many providers throttle or flag high-volume SMTP traffic from unfamiliar IP ranges.

Sending Attachments and HTML Content

The email:send operation accepts multiple email:attachment elements alongside the body, and each attachment can reference a file on disk, a stream from a previous operation, or bytes computed in DataWeave. Set the body's contentType to text/html when you need rich formatting, and remember that most mail clients still render plain text as a fallback, so pairing an HTML body with meaningful subject lines improves deliverability and readability across clients.

Tip: Test outbound email against a disposable inbox service or an SMTP sandbox (such as a provider's sandbox mode) during development, so test runs never accidentally deliver to real customer addresses.
  • Sending and receiving mail use separate global configs: email:smtp-config for outbound, email:imap-config/email:pop3-config for inbound.
  • IMAP supports folder browsing and leaving mail on the server; POP3 is simpler and typically download-and-remove.
  • Always mark-as-read or delete processed messages to prevent a polling listener from reprocessing the same inbox.
  • Use an SMTP sandbox during development so test flows never send real email to customers.

subtopics.title: JMS Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Understand the Mule 4 JMS Connector for publishing and consuming messages from queues and topics, including message selectors and acknowledgement modes.
subtopics.summary: The JMS Connector integrates Mule with message brokers like ActiveMQ or IBM MQ for reliable, asynchronous queue and topic messaging.
subtopics.content_html:
The Java Message Service (JMS) Connector connects Mule applications to enterprise message brokers such as ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, and Anypoint MQ's JMS bridge. It is the go-to choice when integration requires guaranteed delivery, asynchronous decoupling between producer and consumer, or the publish/subscribe pattern across multiple independent listeners.

Configuring the Connection

A jms:config element wraps a connection factory specific to the broker in use, along with a caching strategy and optional reconnection settings.

<jms:config name="JMS_Config">
    <jms:active-mq-connection username="${jms.user}" password="${jms.password}">
        <jms:factory-configuration brokerUrl="${jms.brokerUrl}"/>
    </jms:active-mq-connection>
</jms:config>

Publishing Messages

jms:publish sends the current payload to a named destination, which can be a queue (point-to-point) or a topic (publish/subscribe). The destinationType attribute distinguishes the two.

<flow name="publish-order-event-flow">
    <jms:publish config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.queue" destinationType="QUEUE">
        <jms:message>
            <jms:body>#[output application/json --- payload]</jms:body>
        </jms:message>
    </jms:publish>
</flow>

Listening for Messages

jms:listener triggers a flow whenever a message arrives on a destination. It supports message selectors (a SQL-92-like filter on JMS headers/properties) and configurable acknowledgement modes to control when a message is considered successfully processed.

<flow name="consume-order-events-flow">
    <jms:listener config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.queue" destinationType="QUEUE"
        ackMode="AUTO" selector="priority = 'HIGH'"/>
    <logger message="Processing order: #[payload]"/>
    <db:insert config-ref="Database_Config">
        <db:sql>INSERT INTO order_log (payload) VALUES (:payload)</db:sql>
        <db:input-parameters>#[{payload: write(payload, 'application/json')}]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:insert>
</flow>

Publish-Consume for Request/Reply

The jms:publish-consume operation implements the JMS request/reply pattern: it publishes a message and then blocks waiting for a correlated reply on a temporary or configured reply destination, which is useful when a synchronous response is still required from an asynchronous broker-based backend.

Key Attributes

AttributePurpose
destinationTypeQUEUE for point-to-point or TOPIC for publish/subscribe
ackModeAUTO, MANUAL, DUPS_OK, or transacted acknowledgement
selectorFilters messages by header/property using SQL-92-like syntax
durablePersists a topic subscription so messages are not lost while the consumer is offline
numberOfConsumersNumber of concurrent listener threads for higher throughput
Tip: Use a durable subscription on a topic when every subscriber must eventually receive every message even if it is temporarily disconnected, which is not guaranteed by a non-durable topic subscription.

Dead Letter Queues and Poison Messages

A message that repeatedly fails processing — due to malformed content or a downstream system outage — can be redelivered indefinitely if not handled carefully. Most brokers support a maximum redelivery count after which the message is routed to a dead letter queue, and pairing this broker-level setting with a Mule error handler around the listener's flow gives an integration a clean way to quarantine poison messages instead of looping on them forever.

Transacted Sessions

For flows where message consumption must be atomic with a related database write, the JMS Connector supports transacted sessions so that a message is only acknowledged as consumed once the entire flow, including any database operations, has committed successfully. If the flow fails partway through, the message becomes available for redelivery instead of being lost.

Key Points

  • Queues deliver each message to exactly one consumer; topics broadcast to every active subscriber.
  • Message selectors filter which messages a listener receives without consuming and discarding them manually.
  • Acknowledgement mode controls when a message is considered successfully delivered and removed from the broker.
  • jms:publish-consume enables synchronous request/reply semantics over an inherently asynchronous transport.

subtopics.title: ActiveMQ Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Connect Mule 4 to ActiveMQ using the generic JMS Connector's jms:active-mq-connection, covering broker URLs, listener, publish, and acknowledgment modes.
subtopics.summary: ActiveMQ integration in Mule 4 uses the generic JMS Connector configured with jms:active-mq-connection and an OpenWire broker URL.
subtopics.content_html:
Unlike some of the other messaging systems in this catalog, ActiveMQ doesn't have a connector bearing its own name in Anypoint Exchange. Instead, Mule talks to ActiveMQ through the generic JMS Connector, which speaks the JMS 1.1/2.0 API that ActiveMQ implements. This makes ActiveMQ a natural fit for organizations already running it as an on-premises broker for order queues, event notifications, or decoupling legacy Java EE applications from newer services.

Adding the ActiveMQ Client Library

The JMS Connector needs a JMS provider implementation on the classpath to actually talk to ActiveMQ; add the ActiveMQ client as a Maven dependency alongside the connector.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.activemq</groupId>
    <artifactId>activemq-client</artifactId>
    <version>5.18.3</version>
</dependency>

Global Configuration

The jms:config element takes a jms:active-mq-connection that wires up an ActiveMQ connection factory pointed at a broker URL, typically using the OpenWire protocol on port 61616. You can supply a factory bean directly or reference one built from the connection URL and credentials.

<jms:config name="JMS_Config" doc:name="JMS Config">
    <jms:active-mq-connection username="${amq.username}" password="${secure::amq.password}">
        <jms:factory-configuration brokerUrl="tcp://${amq.host}:61616"/>
    </jms:active-mq-connection>
    <jms:caching-strategy>
        <jms:default-caching/>
    </jms:caching-strategy>
</jms:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
jms:listenerMessage source that subscribes to a queue or topic destination
jms:publishSends a message to a queue or topic
jms:consumePulls a single message synchronously (request-style consumption)
jms:ackManually acknowledges a message when using CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE mode

Example Flow

This flow listens on a queue for incoming order messages, processes them, and publishes a confirmation onto a downstream topic for interested subscribers.

<flow name="amq-order-processing-flow">
    <jms:listener config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.queue" ackMode="AUTO"/>

    <ee:transform doc:name="Enrich order">
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload ++ {processedAt: now()}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>

    <jms:publish config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.confirmed.topic" destinationType="TOPIC"/>
</flow>
Tip: Set ackMode="AUTO" for simple fire-and-forget processing, but switch to MANUAL with an explicit jms:ack call when you need to guarantee a message is only removed from the queue after downstream side effects — like a database write — have succeeded.

Durability and Redelivery

For topics, configure a durable subscriber name if consumers may be offline when a message is published; otherwise messages published while no subscriber is connected are lost. ActiveMQ also supports dead-letter queues for messages that exceed their redelivery count, which is worth pairing with Mule's error handling so poison messages don't loop indefinitely.

Connecting to a Clustered or Failover Broker

Production ActiveMQ deployments are rarely a single node. When the broker runs in a master/slave or network-of-brokers topology, use a failover transport URL instead of a single tcp:// address so the client automatically reconnects to a surviving broker if the primary goes down.

<jms:factory-configuration brokerUrl="failover:(tcp://broker1:61616,tcp://broker2:61616)?randomize=false"/>

This URL syntax tells the ActiveMQ client library to try each broker in order and keep retrying transparently, which is far more resilient than hardcoding a single host and relying on Mule's own reconnection strategy alone.

  • ActiveMQ is accessed through the generic JMS Connector, using jms:active-mq-connection and an OpenWire broker URL, not a dedicated ActiveMQ connector.
  • Choose manual acknowledgment when message loss on downstream failure is unacceptable.
  • Use durable subscriptions on topics so offline consumers don't silently miss messages.
  • Use a failover broker URL in production so the client survives a broker failover without manual intervention.

subtopics.title: Anypoint MQ Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Anypoint MQ Connector with Connected App credentials, covering queues vs exchanges, FIFO queues, publish, and subscriber operations.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint MQ is MuleSoft's managed cloud messaging service, configured with anypoint-mq:config and used through publish, subscriber, ack, and nack operations.
subtopics.content_html:
Anypoint MQ is MuleSoft's own cloud-native messaging service, fully managed within the Anypoint Platform, and it's frequently the default choice when a project is already standardized on CloudHub and doesn't want to stand up and operate a separate broker. Because it's provisioned through Anypoint Platform itself, queues and exchanges are managed the same way as APIs and applications — with environment separation, role-based access, and built-in monitoring in Anypoint Monitoring.

Queues, Exchanges, and FIFO

An Anypoint MQ queue behaves like a standard point-to-point destination. An exchange, paired with one or more bound queues, gives you publish/subscribe fan-out similar to a topic in other brokers. Every queue can be provisioned as either Standard, which prioritizes throughput and allows occasional out-of-order or duplicate delivery, or FIFO, which guarantees strict ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group at the cost of some throughput.

Global Configuration

The anypoint-mq:config element authenticates with a Connected App's client ID and client secret (or legacy queue-level credentials), and it targets a specific Anypoint MQ region and environment tied to your organization.

<anypoint-mq:config name="AnypointMQ_Config" doc:name="Anypoint MQ Config">
    <anypoint-mq:connection clientId="${amq.clientId}" clientSecret="${secure::amq.clientSecret}"
        url="https://mq-us-east-1.anypoint.mulesoft.com/api/v1"/>
</anypoint-mq:config>

Key Operations

OperationPurpose
anypoint-mq:publishPublishes a message to a queue or exchange
anypoint-mq:subscriberMessage source that continuously receives messages from a queue
anypoint-mq:consumePulls a single message on demand rather than continuously
anypoint-mq:ack / anypoint-mq:nackConfirms successful processing or requeues a failed message

Example Flow

This flow publishes a payment event to an exchange for fan-out, and a companion flow subscribes to a bound queue, acknowledging each message only after it's processed successfully.

<flow name="publish-payment-event">
    <anypoint-mq:publish config-ref="AnypointMQ_Config" destination="payments-exchange">
        <anypoint-mq:body>#[write(payload, 'application/json')]</anypoint-mq:body>
    </anypoint-mq:publish>
</flow>
