<flow name="consume-payments-queue" maxConcurrency="4">
    <anypoint-mq:subscriber config-ref="AnypointMQ_Config" destination="payments-notifications-queue"
        acknowledgementMode="MANUAL"/>

    <try>
        <flow-ref name="record-payment-notification"/>
        <anypoint-mq:ack messageAckId="#[attributes.ackId]"/>
    <error-handler>
        <on-error-continue>
            <anypoint-mq:nack messageAckId="#[attributes.ackId]"/>
        </on-error-continue>
    </error-handler>
    </try>
</flow>
Tip: Set maxConcurrency on the flow containing an anypoint-mq:subscriber to control how many messages are processed in parallel, and pair manual acknowledgment with a dead-letter queue so repeatedly failing messages don't block the queue indefinitely.

When to Choose Anypoint MQ

Anypoint MQ removes the operational burden of running and patching a broker, integrates natively with CloudHub networking and security, and is billed per message rather than per server, which suits bursty workloads. Teams with an existing enterprise messaging standard — ActiveMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka — often keep that broker for cross-platform needs and use Anypoint MQ specifically for Mule-to-Mule communication.

Dead-Letter Queues and Monitoring

Every Anypoint MQ queue can be configured with a dead-letter queue that automatically receives messages after they exceed a maximum delivery count, preventing a single malformed message from blocking an otherwise healthy queue. Anypoint Monitoring surfaces queue depth, message age, and throughput out of the box, which makes it straightforward to set an alert when a queue's backlog grows past an expected threshold — often a sign that a downstream consumer has stalled or is failing to acknowledge messages.

Client applications authenticate through a Connected App rather than embedding a static API key, which lets an administrator revoke or rotate access centrally without redeploying every Mule application that publishes or subscribes to a given queue.

  • Choose FIFO queues when strict ordering and exactly-once delivery matter more than raw throughput.
  • Use exchanges when multiple independent queues need a copy of the same published message.
  • Manual acknowledgment combined with a dead-letter queue is the safest pattern for production consumers.
  • Monitor queue depth and message age in Anypoint Monitoring to catch stalled consumers early.

subtopics.title: VM Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Mule 4 VM Connector enables fast, in-memory or persistent queue-based communication between flows inside a single Mule application at runtime.
subtopics.summary: The VM Connector provides fast intra-application messaging through in-memory or persistent queues, ideal for decoupling flows.
subtopics.content_html:
The VM (Virtual Machine) Connector enables communication between flows running inside the same Mule application, or, less commonly, between applications deployed to the same Mule runtime. It behaves much like a lightweight internal message broker without requiring an external JMS provider, making it the natural choice for decoupling processing stages within a single project.

Configuring VM Queues

A vm:config element declares one or more named queues up front. Each queue can be transient (in-memory, lost on restart, fastest) or persistent (backed by disk storage, survives a runtime restart, slightly slower).

<vm:config name="VM_Config">
    <vm:queues>
        <vm:queue queueName="order-processing" queueType="PERSISTENT"/>
        <vm:queue queueName="notification-events" queueType="TRANSIENT"/>
    </vm:queues>
</vm:config>

Publishing Asynchronously

vm:publish sends a message to a queue and immediately continues the calling flow without waiting for it to be processed, which is the classic fire-and-forget decoupling pattern — for example, acknowledging an inbound HTTP request instantly while heavier processing happens on a separate thread.

<flow name="receive-order-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/orders" allowedMethods="POST"/>
    <vm:publish config-ref="VM_Config" queueName="order-processing">
        <vm:content>#[payload]</vm:content>
    </vm:publish>
    <set-payload value="#[output application/json --- {status: 'accepted'}]"/>
</flow>

<flow name="process-order-async-flow">
    <vm:listener config-ref="VM_Config" queueName="order-processing"/>
    <logger message="Processing order asynchronously: #[payload]"/>
</flow>

Synchronous Request/Reply with publish-consume

When the caller needs a result back, vm:publish-consume sends a message and blocks until a response is available from the consuming flow, functioning much like an internal, synchronous flow-ref but across independently scheduled flows.

<flow name="validate-order-flow">
    <vm:publish-consume config-ref="VM_Config" queueName="validation-requests" timeout="5000">
        <vm:content>#[payload]</vm:content>
    </vm:publish-consume>
</flow>

VM vs JMS

AspectVM ConnectorJMS Connector
ScopeSame Mule runtime / applicationAny system with a JMS broker connection
External dependencyNone requiredRequires a message broker (ActiveMQ, IBM MQ, etc.)
PersistenceOptional, disk-backed persistent queuesBroker-managed persistence and clustering
Typical useDecoupling flows within one appCross-application or cross-system messaging
Note: Persistent VM queues add durability but also I/O overhead, so reserve them for messages that genuinely must survive an application restart; use transient queues for high-throughput, best-effort internal messaging.

Typical Design Patterns

A common pattern splits a single logical process into an inbound flow that accepts a request, validates it quickly, and publishes to a VM queue, followed by one or more downstream flows that do the heavier lifting — enrichment, multiple backend calls, retries — independently of the original caller. This keeps the inbound response time low and isolates slow or failure-prone processing so it does not block the API consumer.

VM Queues and CloudHub

On CloudHub, VM queues are scoped to a single worker instance. When an application runs with multiple workers, each worker maintains its own separate VM queues, which means VM is not a substitute for a shared broker like JMS or Anypoint MQ in a horizontally scaled, multi-worker deployment where any worker might need to consume a message published by another.

Key Points

  • VM queues live inside the Mule runtime, requiring no external broker infrastructure.
  • vm:publish is fire-and-forget; vm:publish-consume blocks for a synchronous reply.
  • Persistent queues survive application restarts at the cost of some throughput compared to transient queues.
  • VM is ideal for decoupling processing stages within a single application; JMS is better for cross-system messaging.

subtopics.title: Object Store (ObjectStore V2)
subtopics.meta_description: Use the Mule 4 Object Store connector for persistent and in-memory key-value storage, covering store, retrieve, TTL, and idempotency patterns.
subtopics.summary: The Object Store connector gives Mule flows a simple key-value store for caching, state, and idempotency, either in memory or persisted across CloudHub workers.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every integration problem is about calling an external system — sometimes a flow simply needs somewhere to remember something between messages: a processed message ID, a cached lookup value, a rate-limit counter. The Object Store connector (ObjectStore V2 in current runtimes) provides exactly that: a lightweight key-value store that is available to every Mule application without deploying a separate database.

Persistent vs. Transient Stores

Object stores come in two flavors, and choosing the right one matters for both correctness and cost:

  • Transient (in-memory) — data lives only in the worker's JVM heap and is lost on restart or redeploy. Fast, but not durable and not shared across CloudHub workers unless the deployment is single-worker.
  • Persistent — on CloudHub, backed by MuleSoft's managed Object Store service, which survives restarts, redeploys, and is shared across all workers of an application. On-premises, persistence can be backed by a configured store implementation. Persistent stores are the correct choice for idempotency and any state that must survive a deployment.
Tip: Default application object stores are convenient for prototyping, but define an explicit named `os:object-store` with a clear `partition` and TTL for anything beyond a single flow — it avoids key collisions between unrelated flows sharing the same default store.

Global Configuration

AttributePurpose
persistenttrue for durable storage backed by the Object Store service, false for in-memory only
entryTtl / entryTtlUnitTime-to-live for each entry before automatic expiration, e.g. 24 HOURS
maxEntriesCaps the number of entries, evicting the oldest when exceeded (useful for bounded caches)
expirationInterval / expirationIntervalUnitHow often the store sweeps for expired entries

Key Operations

  • os:store — writes a value under a key, optionally with `failIfPresent` to enforce write-once semantics.
  • os:retrieve — reads a value by key, with a `defaultValue` expression to avoid errors on a cache miss.
  • os:contains — checks key existence without retrieving the value, cheaper for simple duplicate checks.
  • os:remove — deletes a key, commonly used to clear processed markers or invalidate a cache entry.

Example Flow: Idempotent Message Processing

<os:object-store name="Processed_Orders_Store"
    persistent="true"
    entryTtl="7"
    entryTtlUnit="DAYS"/>

<flow name="process-order-flow">
    <jms:listener config-ref="JMS_Config" destination="orders.queue"/>
    <os:contains
        objectStore="Processed_Orders_Store"
        key="#[payload.orderId]"
        target="alreadyProcessed"/>
    <choice>
        <when expression="#[vars.alreadyProcessed]">
            <logger level="INFO" message="#['Duplicate order ' ++ payload.orderId ++ ' skipped']"/>
        </when>
        <otherwise>
            <flow-ref name="submit-order-to-erp-flow"/>
            <os:store
                objectStore="Processed_Orders_Store"
                key="#[payload.orderId]">
                <os:value>#[true]</os:value>
            </os:store>
        </otherwise>
    </choice>
</flow>

Partitioning and Naming Strategy

Every named object store is effectively its own partition, isolated from other stores in the same application. A common pattern is one store per logical concern — a `processed-orders` store for deduplication, a `reference-data-cache` store for slow-changing lookups, a `rate-limit-counters` store for throttling — each with its own TTL tuned to how long that data should realistically live. Mixing unrelated concerns into a single default store makes it harder to reason about expiration behavior and increases the chance that a broad `os:remove` intended for one use case accidentally clears state for another.

Common Use Cases

  • Deduplication and idempotent processing for message-driven flows that may redeliver the same message.
  • Caching results of expensive or rate-limited outbound calls (reference data lookups, token responses).
  • Tracking simple workflow state, such as circuit-breaker counters or last-run watermarks for polling connectors.
  • Storing short-lived OAuth access tokens shared across concurrent flow executions to avoid redundant token requests.

Key Points

  • Always set an appropriate TTL — object stores are not meant to be a permanent database and unbounded growth has real cost and performance implications.
  • Use persistent stores for anything that must survive a redeploy; transient stores are fine for pure in-request caching within a single worker's lifetime.
  • Object Store operations are fast but still add network latency on CloudHub since the store is a managed service — avoid calling it inside tight loops when a local variable would do.
  • Give each object store a clear, scoped name and matching TTL rather than relying on the implicit default application store for everything.

subtopics.title: Web Service Consumer (SOAP) Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Web Service Consumer connector against a WSDL, build SOAP envelopes with DataWeave, and handle WS-Security headers.
subtopics.summary: The Web Service Consumer connector generates callable operations from a WSDL, letting Mule flows invoke SOAP services without hand-writing envelopes.
subtopics.content_html:
Despite the industry's broad shift to REST and JSON, a large share of legacy enterprise systems — mainframes, older ERP modules, government and financial services platforms — still expose only SOAP web services described by a WSDL. The Web Service Consumer connector (WSC) is MuleSoft's general-purpose bridge into that world: point it at a WSDL and it derives the available operations, request and response schemas, and bindings automatically, rather than requiring you to construct raw SOAP XML by hand.

Global Configuration

The connector reads the WSDL at design time to build its operation list, so the WSDL location and the desired service/port must be known upfront.

AttributePurpose
wsdlLocationURL or classpath location of the WSDL document
serviceThe wsdl:service name to use when the WSDL defines more than one
portThe specific port (binding) within the service, e.g. a SOAP 1.1 vs SOAP 1.2 binding
addressOverrides the endpoint address from the WSDL, useful when calling a different environment than the one the WSDL was published from

Authentication is layered on top through a connection provider — HTTP basic authentication for simple services, or a WS-Security configuration for services requiring signed or encrypted SOAP headers (UsernameToken, timestamps, or X.509 signatures).

Tip: When a target service publishes both SOAP 1.1 and 1.2 bindings, prefer 1.2 for better fault handling and MTOM support unless the consumer system explicitly requires 1.1.

Key Operation: Consume

Unlike connectors with many named operations, WSC exposes a single generic wsc:consume operation. You select the target operation by name (as defined in the WSDL's portType), and the connector expects a fully-formed SOAP body as the outgoing payload — typically built with DataWeave targeting XML output that matches the operation's request schema. SOAP headers (including WS-Security tokens) are supplied separately as message properties or through the WS-Security configuration rather than embedded in the payload.

Example Flow

<wsc:config name="LegacyBilling_WSC_Config">
    <wsc:connection
        wsdlLocation="${billing.wsdl.url}"
        service="BillingService"
        port="BillingServiceSoap12"
        address="${billing.endpoint.address}">
        <wsc:web-service-security>
            <wsc:username-token username="${billing.username}" password="${billing.password}"/>
        </wsc:web-service-security>
    </wsc:connection>
</wsc:config>

<flow name="get-invoice-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/invoices/{invoiceId}"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/xml
ns bill http://legacy.acme.com/billing
---
bill#GetInvoiceRequest: {
    bill#InvoiceId: attributes.uriParams.invoiceId
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
    <wsc:consume config-ref="LegacyBilling_WSC_Config" operation="GetInvoice"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
ns bill http://legacy.acme.com/billing
---
{
    invoiceId: payload.Body.GetInvoiceResponse.bill#InvoiceId,
    amountDue: payload.Body.GetInvoiceResponse.bill#AmountDue
}]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
</flow>

Handling SOAP Faults

When the target service returns a SOAP fault instead of a normal response, the connector raises a dedicated WSC:SOAP_FAULT error rather than silently passing the fault envelope through as a success payload. Wrapping the wsc:consume call in an on-error-propagate handler scoped to that error type lets a flow inspect the fault code and fault string and translate them into a meaningful HTTP status and JSON error body for REST consumers, instead of leaking raw SOAP XML back to callers who never expected to see it.

Common Use Cases

  • Wrapping legacy SOAP services (billing, mainframe integrations, older insurance and banking platforms) behind a modern REST facade.
  • Calling government or industry-standard SOAP services that have no REST equivalent.
  • Bridging partner-facing SOAP APIs where WS-Security compliance is mandated by contract.
  • Migrating incrementally off a SOAP backend by fronting it with a REST API while the underlying service is modernized.

Key Points

  • The connector derives its operations from the WSDL at design time, so any WSDL change requires refreshing the connector configuration in Studio.
  • DataWeave's XML output module, including namespace prefixes, is the practical way to build the SOAP body without manual string concatenation.
  • SOAP faults surface as connector errors; catch them explicitly in an error handler to map them into meaningful REST error responses.
  • Cache the address override per environment so the same WSDL-derived configuration can point at sandbox, UAT, and production endpoints without redesigning the flow.

subtopics.title: Apache Kafka Connector
subtopics.meta_description: Configure the Mule 4 Apache Kafka Connector producer and consumer configs, publish and listen to topics, and manage consumer groups and serialization.
subtopics.summary: The Apache Kafka Connector lets Mule applications publish to and consume from Kafka topics with configurable serialization and consumer group semantics.
subtopics.content_html:
Apache Kafka has become the default backbone for high-throughput, event-driven architectures, and MuleSoft applications frequently need to sit on either side of it — publishing domain events for other systems to consume, or reacting to a stream of events produced elsewhere. The Kafka Connector gives Mule flows native producer and consumer capabilities without requiring a hand-rolled Java client wrapped in a custom component.

Producer and Consumer Configurations

Kafka's client model separates producing and consuming cleanly, and the connector mirrors that with two distinct global configuration elements rather than one shared config.

Config ElementKey Attributes
kafka:producer-configbootstrapServers, keySerializer, valueSerializer, acks (0/1/all), compressionType
kafka:consumer-configbootstrapServers, keyDeserializer, valueDeserializer, consumerGroupId, autoOffsetReset (earliest/latest)

bootstrapServers is a comma-separated list of one or more broker host:port pairs used only to discover the rest of the cluster, so it does not need to list every broker. For secured clusters, both configs also accept SASL/SSL security properties (security.protocol, sasl.mechanism, truststore location) matching whatever the Kafka cluster enforces.

Note: String and JSON payloads are the simplest to start with using StringSerializer/StringDeserializer, but production systems handling schema evolution typically move to Avro with a schema registry, which requires the corresponding Avro serializer/deserializer classes on the classpath.

Key Operations and Sources

  • kafka:publish — sends a message to a named topic, optionally with a partition key to control which partition the message lands on (important for maintaining per-key ordering).
  • kafka:message-listener — a message source that subscribes to one or more topics as part of a consumer group, triggering a flow for each record (or batch of records, depending on configuration) received.
  • kafka:commit — used when the listener is configured for manual offset commits, giving the flow control over exactly when an offset is considered processed.

Example Flow

<kafka:producer-config name="Kafka_Producer_Config">
    <kafka:producer-connection
        bootstrapServers="${kafka.brokers}"
        keySerializer="org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer"
        valueSerializer="org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer"/>
</kafka:producer-config>

<kafka:consumer-config name="Kafka_Consumer_Config">
    <kafka:consumer-connection
        bootstrapServers="${kafka.brokers}"
        keyDeserializer="org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer"
        valueDeserializer="org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer"
        consumerGroupId="order-events-consumer"
        autoOffsetReset="EARLIEST"/>
</kafka:consumer-config>

<flow name="publish-order-event-flow">
    <http:listener config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" path="/orders"/>
    <kafka:publish
        config-ref="Kafka_Producer_Config"
        topic="order-events"
        key="#[payload.orderId]">
        <kafka:message>#[write(payload, 'application/json')]</kafka:message>
    </kafka:publish>
</flow>

<flow name="consume-order-events-flow">
    <kafka:message-listener
        config-ref="Kafka_Consumer_Config"
        topics="order-events"/>
    <ee:transform>
        <ee:message>
            <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
read(payload, 'application/json')]]></ee:set-payload>
        </ee:message>
    </ee:transform>
    <flow-ref name="apply-order-to-fulfillment-flow"/>
</flow>

Scaling Consumers

Because Kafka assigns each partition of a topic to at most one consumer within a given consumer group at a time, the practical unit of parallelism is the partition count, not the number of deployed Mule workers. If a topic has six partitions, running more than six instances of a listener sharing the same consumer group leaves the extra instances idle. Plan topic partition counts with expected consumer scale in mind, and remember that CloudHub workers running the same application with the same consumer group ID automatically share the topic's partitions rather than each processing every message.

Common Use Cases

  • Publishing domain events (order placed, inventory updated) for downstream microservices to react to asynchronously.
  • Consuming clickstream, IoT, or log event topics for real-time enrichment and routing.
  • Bridging Kafka topics into REST or database sinks as part of a broader event-streaming platform.
  • Feeding an audit or event-sourcing store by consuming every event published to a set of business topics.

Key Points

  • Use a partition key that matches your ordering requirements — messages with the same key always land on the same partition and preserve order within it.
  • Consumer group ID determines how work is balanced across listener instances; multiple instances sharing a group ID split the topic's partitions between them.
  • Choose acks and offset commit strategy deliberately: acks=all with manual commits trades some throughput for stronger delivery guarantees.
  • Size topic partitions with future consumer scale in mind, since partition count is the hard ceiling on parallel consumption within a group.
